Maybe you should try actually reading that link, because the case wasn't at all like what you described.

Comcast wasn't blocking access to certain websites. They were slowing download speeds from peer-to-peer networks. And it wasn't at the request of a competitor or politically-motivated. It was because of their own incompetence: they couldn't handle all the bandwidth that P2P networks were using. What they were doing was illegal and unethical, but it wasn't censorship. The only thing they were trying to hide was how shitty their service was.

I still have yet to see any evidence for the ISP-driven censorship that supposedly requires government intervention.

If you don't think that blocking access is censorship then we disagree. To me, blocking one type of traffic is the same as blocking one type of website. If you allow ISPs to block peer-to-peer traffic because its too popular, what stops them from banning websites because they are popular? And then what stops them from banning traffic to places they just plain don't like? Maybe I'm being paranoid.

I didn't say that blocking access isn't censorship. I said that they weren't blocking access. Comcast wasn't preventing anyone from using P2P networks at all, they were just slowing their download speeds. It was less about popularity and more about P2P hogging a lot of bandwidth and Comcast being too incompetent and lazy to handle that without screwing over their customers.

The type of situation that net neutrality advocates are talking about would be more like The Pirate Bay going to Comcast and convincing them to block Soulseek (or at least start charging Soulseek users extra).

To be clear: I'm not defending what Comcast did. They were clearly in the wrong and deserved to be slapped down in court. I'm just pointing out that what they did isn't actually an example of what net neutrality advocates claim ISPs want to do.
